builder_plan.scenario: An agent reads external documents or tool responses that may contain malicious instructions.
builder_plan.change: Replay attacks and legitimate lookalikes in an isolated copy of your agent workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your existing checks with the same tasks, permissions, and tool responses.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful attacks missed, legitimate actions blocked, detection delay, and review cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: SparLeak: Privacy Leakage from Sparse Attention in LLM Inference on Shared GPUs
summary: This is an attack, not a defense: it replaces no production technique, but demonstrates that sparse attention's input-dependent KV-cache access patterns leak query attributes and response content to a co-located adversary on a shared GPU. Exploiting or mitigating it costs engineering effort in monitoring, GPU isolation, or modifications to sparse attention kernels; the attack itself requires profiling infrastructure, trained attack models, and co-location with the victim. Adoption of mitigations can fail if defenses perturb sparsity patterns only partially, degrade the latency benefits that motivated sparse attention, or assume threat models where the attacker lacks shared-GPU access.
rationale: The reader running a single 24 GB GPU or third-party APIs is more likely a potential victim than an attacker, so the actionable step is awareness and deployment hygiene rather than adoption: avoid untrusted co-tenancy on shared GPUs when serving sparse-attention models with sensitive data.
technique: Side-channel attack on sparse-attention GPU memory access

claims.statement: This is an attack, not a defense: it replaces no production technique, but demonstrates that sparse attention's input-dependent KV-cache access patterns leak query attributes and response content to a co-located adversary on a shared GPU. Exploiting or mitigating it costs engineering effort in monitoring, GPU isolation, or modifications to sparse attention kernels; the attack itself requires profiling infrastructure, trained attack models, and co-location with the victim. Adoption of mitigations can fail if defenses perturb sparsity patterns only partially, degrade the latency benefits that motivated sparse attention, or assume threat models where the attacker lacks shared-GPU access.

SparLeak achieves average attack success rates of 90.9% for query attribute inference and 87.3% for response reconstruction across three LLM architectures, three sparse attention mechanisms, and three privacy-sensitive datasets.
